svg.text: How ux.md works with the Intent Spec
Two documents, one direction of travel. The gate files hold the thinking. The Intent Spec holds the decision and the signature.
THE THINKING — UNSIGNED, AND STILL CHANGING
ux.md
Do we understand the problem · Is this the right thing to build
The problem, and whose it is
The tasks people are actually trying to finish
THE OPTIONS — more than one, side by side
WHAT WE RULED OUT, AND WHY
THE EVIDENCE — which claim rests on which finding
Always required. Every project has a problem and some state of knowledge about it.
design.md
Is this one built right
Who uses it, to do what, where, under what pressure
ACCESSIBILITY — the standard, the scope, who audits it
APEX — real components, bound tokens, the canonical view
How it gets tested, and the number that counts as passing
Optional — but a project with no Gate 3 has to SAY so. Silence is what's disallowed.
Both are one person's reading of the same evidence.
Neither is signed, on purpose — a reading that is still changing cannot sit inside a signed document.
THE DECISION — SIGNED, AND BINDING
The Intent Spec
You already have this. Nothing here replaces it or competes with it.
Requirements — ONE canonical list, not four
What success looks like, and what would count as failing
Why this work exists at all
Who it is for, and who else is affected
What is explicitly out of scope
What must never break, vs. what should be good
Open questions · how it gets tested · what evidence is required
The decision log, and the signatures
The one rule, and why it matters:
a gate file POINTS at this. It never restates it. Anything written in
both places drifts apart — and the unsigned copy wins by accident,
because it is the one people are actually editing.
A pointer is only honest if the thing it points at is filled in.
Replacing a real sentence with "see the Intent Spec" is worse than repeating it, if the spec still says TBD.
Six of the fourteen sections first proposed for the gate files turned out to belong here, and became pointers.
every requirement id
resolves to one row here
direction · non-goals
metrics · decisions
— read from here,
never copied over
"WHY NOT JUST PUT ALL THIS IN THE SPEC?" — FOUR THINGS IT HAS NOWHERE TO PUT
1 · The receipts
A contract says what we will
build. It has no line for
piece of evidence — so nobody
can check one without you.
2 · More than one idea
It holds a single answer,
because that is what a
commitment is. Early on you
need three or four options
next to each other.
3 · The ideas that lost
It records what was decided,
not what was considered and
dropped. So the same idea
gets pitched again next
quarter, and argued again.
4 · Fact vs. reading
It states things plainly —
that is its job. It cannot
show the difference between
"we watched people do this"
and "this is our reading".
Beth Connor · 2026-09-22 · ux.md answers Gates 1 and 2 in one file. design.md answers Gate 3, which is a different question: not what should exist, but whether this one is built right.
Spec-driven tooling was written for code. A code spec may assume itself correct and check the build against it. A claim about people may not — which is what the left-hand column is for.
